description-catchment: Natural catchment including rugged uplands. Impermeable bedrock (Ordovician shales and greywackes) overlain with superficial deposits. Extensive forestry (Glentrool Forest); several lochs.
description-flow-regime: NA

name: Water of Fleet at Rusko
description-summary: A velocity-area station on the Water of Fleet, upstream of Gatehouse of Fleet.
description-general: Velocity area station on short straight reach with gravel bed and gravel shoal control.
description-station-hydrometry: Flows well contained with help from rh floodbank. New rating applied since 10/10/2008 when a flood event resulted in control change.
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: Predominatly low-lying catchment. Impermeable bedrock (Silurian shales with granitic intrusion which forms highest point in catchment at Cairnsmore of Fleet); overlain with superficial deposits. Rugged moorland catchment with extensive forestry.
description-flow-regime: NA

name: Girvan at Robstone
description-summary: Velocity area station on the River Girvan. Flows affected by abstractions from Loch Bradan.
description-general: Velocity area station approx. 15m wide.
description-station-hydrometry: Low flow control is an informal gravel weir built in 1982, which is subject to re-grading in substantial floods. Flood banks contain all flows (pre-1982, right bank inundated beyond 2.2m). Peak flow ratings from current meter gaugings. Rating for period up to 1982 max gauging 2.2m (about 0.9 QMED); post-1982 max gauging up to 1.9m (about 0.7 QMED), simple extrapolation beyond. Gaugings to 1982 show scatter; may suggest a changing relationship.
description-flow-record: Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in September 2022 (WINFAP Files v11).
description-catchment: Upland catchment draining from Carrick Forest. Complex geology: Ordovician/Carboniferous metamorphics and igneous formations; predominantly overlain by superficial deposits, drift and peat also. Mostly hill pasture with some mixed farming in the valley and afforestation in the headwaters; several lochs.
description-flow-regime: Runoff diminished by abstractions from Loch Bradan. Additional storage in a few high level lochs.

name: Doon at Auchendrane
description-summary: A velocity-area station on the River Doon to the South of Prestwick.
description-general: Velocity area station in a straight section.
description-station-hydrometry: Riffle control at low flows, rock boulder control at high discharges. Wide floodplain u/s but all flows contained.
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: Mostly upland catchment developed on basement rocks - metamorphosed sediments (Ordovician and Carboniferous) and igneous formations; >60% covered by superficial deposits. Hill pasture is the principal land use, some afforestation - mostly in headwaters. Significant extent of lochs.
description-flow-regime: Flow regime heavily influenced by regulation releases from Loch Doon (129.5 sq.km) - large export of water reduces runoff substantially.

name: Stinchar at Balnowlart
description-summary: Velocity area station in a rural catchment with extensive forested upland areas in the west.
description-general: Velocity area station in long straight reach. Approx. 20m wide section.
description-station-hydrometry: Riffle control. All but exceptional floods contained (<3.1m). Peak flow ratings derived from current meter gaugings up to 3 m (about 0.9 QMED), simple extrapolation beyond. Hydrometric performance has been modestly affected by a leaking stilling well, known to still be leaking as of Jan 2010, although extent of effect on hydrometric performance is unknown.
description-flow-record: Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in September 2023 (WINFAP Files v12).
description-catchment: Catchment topography approx. 2/3 lowland and 1/3 upland. Predominantly impermeable bedrock dominated by metamorphosed sandstone and shales (Ordovician) with igneous outcrops in the headwaters, overlain with Peat and Boulder Clay. Rural catchment with extensive forested upland areas in W (Carrick Forest); hill pasture elsewhere. Afforestation.
description-flow-regime: PWS abstractions cause small reduction in runoff. Very limited storage within the catchment.

name: Garnock at Dalry
description-summary: A velocity-area station downstream of the Muirhead and Camphill Reservoirs.
description-general: River section 0.8km d/s of Dalry. Station added to peak flows dataset in September 2023 (WINFAP Files v12).
description-station-hydrometry: After a long period of closure, the station was reopened on 21/11/2014 to inform flood management. The new station infrastructure is situated on top of the original station plinth. The station is gauged up to 2.657m, with a measured flow of 57.7 cumecs. The rating has been extended by flow modelling to increase the confidence of flood estimation. The new station has a different datum from the original site.
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: NA
description-flow-regime: Runoff substantially reduced by PWS exports from u/s reservoirs.

name: Ayr at Catrine
description-summary: Velocity area station. Flows modestly affected by hydro-electric power scheme.
description-general: Velocity area station (approx. 20m wide) in a long straight reach. There is a flood bank on the lb and retaining wall on the rb.
description-station-hydrometry: The low to medium flow control is an informal broad-crested weir. At higher flows when the weir drowns out, natural channel features will become more prevalent including some sharp bends in the river downstream. Old Howford Bridge 1.5k downstream may be a influential control feature at very high flows. All flows are contained in the channel. Peak flow ratings derived from current meter gaugings up to 1.5m and are based on simple extrapolation beyond this stage.
description-flow-record: Missing data during May 2021 due to weir collapse. Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in August 2021 (WINFAP Files v10).
description-catchment: A catchment of rugged topography draining W from Southern Uplands. Complex bedrock - Carboniferous sediments and igneous outcrops dominate; extensive superficial deposits (mostly Boulder Clay and peat). Hill grazing is the main land use; some forestry. No significant catchment changes known.
description-flow-regime: A responsive, natural catchment but the flow pattern is modestly affected (especially at low flows) by the operation of a small hydro-electric power scheme 1km upstream. Some open cast mining in upper areas.

name: Lugar Water at Langholm
description-summary: Velocity area station in a very responsive, natural and mostly upland catchment.
description-general: Velocity area station; approx. 15m wide.
description-station-hydrometry: Langholm gauging station, referred to locally as Langholm A, worked in tandem with Langholm B station between 1979 and 1990. Langholm B was in the mill lade that bypassed Langholm A and measured flows via a thin-plate weir. The two flows were then combined to produce a mean daily flow record. Although the amount of bypassing is thought to be minimal for all but the most extreme floods, and even less so post 1990 when thereafter the upstream sluice and lade is assumed to have remained closed, the bypassing element is not well understood. Langholm B station datum level is noted as 84.17mOD. The control at Langholm A was originally an informal manmade rock/boulder structure that now takes the form of a man-made riffle. A major shift in the stage flow relationship through the full range in the early 1980s is attributed to a succession of floods that collapsed the control, with gauging evidence pointing to the event of 04/01/1982 as being the decisive event to apply a rating shift from. The rock control was repaired on 08/08/1983, giving a rise in stage of 0.063m. This repair does not prompt a rating shift as expected. It is possible the repair failed rapidly, but this oddity is one of many factors that contribute to the uncertainty in the flood estimations from this station. Other factors include the unexplained weak relationship of available flood gaugings. In summary, there is poor confidence in flow estimations above around 70 cumecs. One peak flow rating across period of record.
description-flow-record: Flows from Jan 2002 reprocessed in 2012. Icing evident in hydrograph 1-14/1/2011. Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in August 2026 (WINFAP Files v15).
description-catchment: A mostly upland catchment developed, mainly, on Carboniferous sediments (chiefly Coal Measures) and igneous formations; extensively overlain by superficial deposits. Hill grazing is the major landuse with some forestry. No significant catchment changes known.
description-flow-regime: Very responsive, natural catchment (open cast mines and minor effluent discharge close to the station).

name: Irvine at Shewalton
description-summary: Velocity area station with bank stability issues since March 2011.
description-general: Velocity area station approx. 30m wide.
description-station-hydrometry: Flows are largely contained in the channel. The station has an open channel control and a rock bar and road bridge approximately 600m downstream are likely key features in the high flow control. Foundations of a mill weir 400m downstream may also survive as a stubborn bed control feature. The flood rating QHigh1973 applied through the record up to the 2011 datum change is informed by gauging up to 3.81m (measured flow of 324 cumecs) and then based on simple extrapolation thereafter. The flood rating QHigh2011 applied after the 2011 datum change is informed by gaugings up to 3.463m (measured flow of 156 cumecs) and then benefits from upper segment that are derived from hydraulic modelling. The station starts operating in July 1972 and the digital record currently starts from 01/03/1978. The historic daily mean flow is the only flow record currently available from 1972. The calculation of 15min resolution flow and Peak Flow series before 01/03/1978 is subject to the future digitising of paper records. A fragment of punch tape data and contemporary gaugings indicate a major datum or control change between February 1973 and February 1974. A potential datum shift is not recorded in SEPA's station history notes and a full understanding will not be possible until paper records are digitised. Another possibility is a major control shift. A written note of 'dam repair' on a chart from 19/05/1973 is odd as a dam currently doesn't exist downstream. However, historic maps show a mill weir did exist approximately 400m downstream and it's possible this feature was still in existence in 1972-1973 and fragments of the foundation likely survive as a bed riffle feature. The station was rebuilt on the same footprint in 2011 to mitigate bank slumping. The works included a new well, hut, ramp gauge and the reprofiling of the bank at the station. The civil works were completed by 14/03/2011. The new stilling well was initially dipped until the new ramp was set up and operational on 14/11/2011. The ramp gauge was set to a new datum from this date. However, a jump in stage is not apparent until 21/11/2011 08:15 and so the rating shift was applied from the 21st to avoid a jump in the flow record. The stage plot shows a gradual increase in base level from around 2003 until 2011 and it is possible this reflects a gradual slump of the old ramp gauge rather than an increase in the bed control. This uncertainty is compensated by rating changes since 2003. The gaugings and stage in this period are aligned to the same ramp readings and hence the flow record on this period is deemed reliable despite the uncertainty around the reference gauge. The period of bank instability between 2003 and 2011 is complicit with issues recording stage in the stilling well, with discrepancies between the well and river level first noted from around March 2008. These issues were linked to the bank instability and water ingress from historic drainage pipes into the stilling well. The poor performance of the well between 2008 and 2011 has been corrected by stage edits informed by monthly visits and calibration against the ramp. In this period of poor well performance, the only period of stage data marked as suspect is between 03/02/11 and 01/11/11, where editing did not satisfy the hydrologist during the quality control of the data. This period coincides with the AMAX flow events in water years 2010 and 2011. Despite this lower confidence in the station performance in 2010 and 2011, the flood estimates most likely remain reasonable and have not been flagged for exclusion in the Peak Flow record. The station stilling well issues resurfaced in 2019 and a pressure level sensor was installed directly in the river on 20/09/2019 to replace the stilling well as the primary source of level data, effectively making the stilling well redundant.
description-flow-record: Flows rejected between 1971 and 1977 pending digitisation and investigation of datum shift. The flow record between 2008 and 2019 is of reduced confidence due to challenges recording stage, where bank instability and seepage of groundwater drainage into the stilling well impacted its performance. The reference ramp gauge may also have been impacted by the bank instability. The stage record was edited into a useable state, but the reduced confidence is worth noting by any user of the dataset. Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in August 2025 (WINFAP Files v14).
description-catchment: Generally upland catchment but topography more subdued below Greenholm. Bedrock predominantly Carboniferous sediments with basalt tracts towards headwaters. Extensively overlain by superficial deposits, mainly Boulder Clay with peat in the headwaters. Land use: mixed farming and hill grazing; some forestry in the upper catchment. Kilmarnock (12km u/s) is the only large urban area.
description-flow-regime: A responsive, sensibly natural flow regime (but affected by effluent from STW). In the near future there is a comprehensive flood prevention scheme planned.

name: Ayr at Mainholm
description-summary: Velocity area station, lowest on the River Ayr. Winter icing can affect flows.
description-general: Velocity area station approx. 30m wide located in a long straight section. Very steep banks (approx. 6m); most flows contained - overspilling occurs on lb.
description-station-hydrometry: Channel control. Rating derived from current meter gaugings up to 3.6m (about QMED), simple extrapolation beyond. Lower end of ratings (<0.615m) recalibrated in 2006 as gaugings since 2001 showed flows were being slightly overestimated.
description-flow-record: December 1981 flows may be affected by ice build-up and are under review. Severe icing in December 2010 led to ice floes in river and stage increase of c.1m at station - flows are estimated. Flows since Jan 2000 reprocessed in 2012. Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in September 2023 (WINFAP Files v12).
description-catchment: Catchment topography approx. 2/3 lowland and 1/3 upland. Complex bedrock geology; Carboniferous sediments (chiefly Coal Measures) dominate, but some igneous formations and Permian sandstones in upper reaches. Extensively overlain by superficial deposits (mostly Boulder Clay and peat). No major urban centres. Hill grazing and forestry in upland headwaters, mixed farming in lowlands. No significant catchment changes known although previously mined for coal.
description-flow-regime: Responsive, natural catchment.

name: Lugton Water at Eglinton Castle
description-summary: A velocity-area station in a linear, mostly lowland catchment.
description-general: Velocity area station with a wide floodplain.
description-station-hydrometry: Cableway (in a straight reach) used for rating. Broad-crested masonry weir as control. Insensitive at low flows; algae can accumulate on crest and cause flow drops on removal (e.g. June 2008 and June 2009).
description-flow-record: A new fish pass was installed in 2018 causing a datum change.
description-catchment: A linear, mostly lowland, catchment. Impervious basalts dominate the headwaters, Carboniferous sediments below; with significant cover by superficial deposits. Land use: predominantly grassland, some forestry and agriculture. Loch Libo, in the upper reaches, has little effect on flows.
description-flow-regime: Very responsive flow pattern.

name: Annick Water at Dreghorn
description-summary: A velocity-area station on the Annick Water in a lowland catchment.
description-general: Velocity area station.
description-station-hydrometry: Some control from a bridge 30m d/s. Various temporary controls have been sited in the river following the removal of an earlier weir (Jul 1982). Calibration checked regularly. Lack of gaugings since 2012 has led to recommended caution for flow beyond about 5 cumecs.
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: Lowland catchment. Bedrock mainly Coal Measures overlain by Boulder Clay, with river terraces and raised beach deposits along river channel. Land use predominantly grazing with isolated forested areas. Urbanisation limited to Stewarton and Irvine.
description-flow-regime: Long Loch and Corsehouse Res. can affect the flow regime.

name: Garnock at Kilwinning
description-summary: A velocity-area station in a very responsive catchment with stage measurement uncertainty since August 2009.
description-general: A velocity-area station.
description-station-hydrometry: River section with long round-crested masonry weir (with central rectangular notch) acting as the control. All flows contained. Exceptionally high tides may influence water levels. No gaugings below 0.6 cumecs and weir deterioration means that flows below 2.0 cumecs should be treated with extreme caution. Stage measurements are subject to further uncertainty since August 2009 due to issues with subsidence and vandalism.
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: Rugged upland headwaters (peat and Boulder Clay overlying igneous formations), mostly Carboniferous sediments covered by superficial deposits in lower catchment. Mainly rural with urbanisation along main valley at Kilbirnie, Dalry and Kilwinning; some forestry.
description-flow-regime: Very responsive catchment notwithstanding several reservoirs (including Muirhead and Camphill) in the headwaters - small net diminution in runoff.

name: Irvine at Newmilns
description-summary: A flat v weir station to the East of Kilmarnock.
description-general: Flat V weir within broad-crested flanks in a long straight reach. Stage data collected for this site dates back to 1959. Station added to peak flows dataset in September 2023 (WINFAP Files v12).
description-station-hydrometry: Weir superseded (Sep 1976) an unstable gravel bar control. Rating based on gaugings up to c.40 cumecs, a daily mean flow which has only been exceeded on 2 consecutive days in the record.
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: Mostly upland catchment developed on basalts and metamorphosed sedimentary formations (mostly Carboniferous and ORS); extensively overlain by superficial deposits. Moorland and rough pasture predominate, significant afforestation in the north, mixed farming in the valley - Greenholm and Darvel are the largest settlements.
description-flow-regime: Sensibly natural flow regime.

name: Ayr at Wellwood
description-summary: A station set-up for a coal project, closed in April 2010.
description-general: Station set-up for a coal project. Station closed April 2010.
description-station-hydrometry: NA
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: Mid-altitude catchment (>200 m). Land use is mostly grasslands and heath.
description-flow-regime: Rather responsive catchment.

name: Gass Water at Welltrees
description-summary: A station set-up for a coal project, closed in December 2006.
description-general: Station set-up for a coal project. Station closed December 2006.
description-station-hydrometry: NA
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: Mid-altitude catchment (>200 m). Predominantly permeable bedrock with extensive impermeable superficial deposits. Land use is mostly grasslands and heath.
description-flow-regime: Rather responsive catchment.

name: Irvine at Glenfield
description-summary: Broad crested masonry weir on the River Irvine.
description-general: The stage record between 1913 and 1981 was recorded by Glenfield and Kennedy engineering works, who manufactured charts recorders and other water engineering components. Although the charts have been digitised by SEPA, there is a significant amount of work required to quality control and prepare the early record for Peak Flow calculation and hence the Peak Flow record is currently only recommended from 1982. Peaks in the 1913 to 1981 period were derived manually from the charts for the original flood studies project and although these records remain published in the Peak Flow dataset, the record will remain flagged as 'rejected' until a full QC can be carried out. Stage recording in the Water Tower was handed over to the Clyde River Purification Board (predecessor of SEPA) in 1982. After issues with the engineering works occasionally closing the inlet pipe of the Water Tower during floods, CRPB installed a second stage recorder in 2002 slightly upstream on a footbridge. The footbridge location initially failed to record lower levels due to siltation of the stilling well (plastic pipe attached to the bridge) and so the two sites worked in tandem until 2010 when recording ceased from the water tower. This was possible after the plastic pipe at the footbridge was replaced with a pressure transducer in 2004. The period of tandem operation had the consequence of two stations being created in SEPA hydrometric database; called Glenfield Water Tower and Glenfield Footbridge. To facilitate the calculation of a single flow archive, a third unified site was created in the SEPA database called Glenfield, which merged all the stage record. This single site approach is consistent with the NRFA holdings where there has only ever been one station called 'Glenfield'. Although the digital record starts on 01/05/1982, significant gaps in the early years mean that a POT series is currently not available before 01/10/1992; a gap between 18/05/85 and 11/07/1985 likely has two missing POT events, a gap between 01/10/86 and 01/11/86 likely has one missing POT event and a gap between 01/01/1992 and 05/02/1992 likely has two missing POT events as well as missing the AMAX event for WY1991. The credible AMAX record begins from 01/10/1982 but with the AMAX figure for 1991 missing.
description-station-hydrometry: The control through the record is a masonry weir, originally constructed for a sluice and lade system for power generation, which is now redundant. Routine sluice openings until the 1970s caused evident dropouts in stage records. The flat-crested weir is inadequate for low flow estimation, so flows below 0.3m are flagged as suspect. The published datum history reflects available notes and understanding as of August 2024. The early period of operation by Glenfield and Kennedy between 1913 and 1981 recorded levels above the crest of the weir. There was an old imperial gauge board opposite the original location of stage recording (water tower) that is assumed to have been zeroed to the weir crest. The weir crest itself consists of large masonry blocks with gaps in-between. The station record review by SEPA in 2024 concluded that the figure of 20.78 mAOD should remain as the gauge zero figure for the period between 1913 and 1981, which is thought to reflect the weir crest and the imperial gauge board zero. A new gauge board was installed at the onset of operation by the River Clyde Purification Board in 1982 and the gauge zero is recorded as 20.589mAOD. The station operation was transferred to SEPA in 1996 who replaced the gauge board with a ramp gauge in September 2004. The gauge zero remained unchanged during this upgrade to a ramp gauge. The gauging station section is lined by flood defence walls that were raised around 2000 to effectively contain the highest events. The exact date and stage of the flood defence works needs to be further investigated. Until this information is available, an estimation of 01/01/2000 will be adopted as the date when the flood walls were raised. The earlier date when the original lower walls were built also needs to be determined so that the differences in channel containment can be reflected in the calibration through the flow record. Rating 3.2 provides confident flood estimations after the flood defence walls were raised, being informed by gaugings up to 2.3m (measured at 113.2 cumecs) and by fluvial modelling for the out of bank segment up to the top of the flood defence walls. Rating 2.1 is applied prior to the second phase of engineering works to convey the reduced confidence in calibration, being a copy of rating 3.2 with the upper limits lowered to flag the out of bank flows as suspect. The segment change point of rating 3.2 indicates the top of the channel to be around 2.048m, but this needs to be further checked by survey. Although rating 2.1 is currently flagged as suspect after 2.048m, this is probably a precautionary approach as the original walls form the foundation of the current wall and the flows will have been contained for a decent height above 2.048m. The original Peak Flow calculations between 1913 and 1981 were derived by a hydraulic formula with correction for drowning and skewness of the weir and with checks against medium range gaugings. The in-channel calibration from rating 3.1 (up to ~ 2m) is deemed an improved rating for this period, and considering the continuity that the weir control provides, it is the intention to recalculate the flows between 1913 and 1981 using a datum adjusted version of rating 3.1. This can only be done after the early-stage record has been quality controlled and until then the flow estimates will be marked as excluded in the Peak Flow record. Largest events in the early period inundated the inside of the meander where the station is positioned, with water flowing across the meander neck and bypassing the station. This is noted as happening during the floods of 03/01/1932 and 08/08/1961. The construction of flood walls means that bypassing is less of a feature after around 1990. Peaks in the 1913 to 1981 period were derived manually from the charts for the original flood studies project and although these records remain published in the peak flow dataset, the record will remain flagged as rejected until a full QC can be carried out.
description-flow-record: Peaks in the 1913 to 1981 period were derived manually from the charts for the original flood studies project and although these records remain published in the peak flow dataset, the record will remain flagged as rejected until a full QC can be carried out. Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in August 2025 (WINFAP Files v14).
description-catchment: Mostly lowland catchment. Predominantly Carboniferous and igneous bedrock, with localised ORS; extensively overlain by superficial deposits (mainly Boulder Clay). Rural catchment with forested areas in NE and urbanisation along main valley (Darvel, Newmilns, Galston and Kilmarnock). Flood walls built approximately spring 1998.
description-flow-regime: A largely natural flow regime but the extent of agricultural flood levees in the catchment will likely have increased from the start of the record.

name: Kelvin at Killermont
description-summary: Velocity area station affected by vigorous seasonal weed growth.
description-general: Velocity area station; approx. 20m wide. Station moved 300m u/s (from Killermont) in 1962.
description-station-hydrometry: Low flow control was unstable gravel control 40m d/s; replaced by gabion weir in Aug 1989. It was subsequently capped with concrete and the upstream face lined with sheet piling, this was completed on the Sept 1995. High flow control was a small island in mid-channel immediately below station; now it is probably the channel bend d/s. The banks have contained all recorded flows. Multiple peak flow ratings across period of record derived from current meter gaugings, simple extrapolation beyond. There is particularly low confidence in the extrapolated flow due to likely backing up from the road bridge downstream and resistance in the woody floodplain.
description-flow-record: Some monthly naturalised flows available (1970-74). Pre-1962 data is rejected because the gauging station was moved 300m upstream. Very low confidence in the accuracy of AMAX1 (1994) due to the exceptionally high magnitude; complex interaction with wooded banks and possible backing up from downstream bridge. Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in April 2017 (WINFAP Files v5).
description-catchment: Predominantly lowland catchment, some upland headwaters in the Campsie Fells. The main channel runs along the northern edge of the Central Lowlands taking tributaries from the faulted igneous block to the north - remainder of catchment is chiefly Carboniferous sediments overlain by, predominantly, Boulder Clay. Mixed land use - moorland, forestry and urban concentrations. A number of small lochs. Notable floodplains. Flood prevention schemes along the river (e.g. at Kirkintilloch, completed March 2003), more projected in the future.
description-flow-regime: Extensive canalisation of river with the Forth and Clyde canal draining through catchment; feeders probably only influence low flows. Effluent return. Mugdock and Craigmaddie Reservoirs for PWS transit water from Loch Katrine via pipelines, probably no effect on Kelvin catchment.

name: Calder at Muirshiel
description-summary: Compound sharp-edged weir. Poor quality and patchy record.
description-general: Compound sharp-edged weir approx. 20m wide. 7km above the river outfall to Castle Semple Loch. Station closed in 1976. SEPA re-opened the station in Dec 1993 with main purpose of pollution prevention and control; but the data is of poor quality. Re-opened station closed in 2003.
description-station-hydrometry: U/s of station is a very active gravel/silt bank. Limit of measurement 16cumecs; no information on hydrometric performance. Theoretical rating (Lea rated).
description-flow-record: Calder Reservoir was breached in 1984, it controlled about 50% of the catchment. Very patchy record but includes most of the 1950s-60s.
description-catchment: Carboniferous basalt on igneous intrusions, overlain by Boulder Clay. Peat in some upland areas. Upland catchment. Land use comprises of moorland and rough grazing. No significant catchment changes known.
description-flow-regime: Very flashy response. Runoff reduced by major u/s abstraction.

name: Clyde at Hazelbank
description-summary: Velocity area station in Southern Uplands. Hydro-electric power upstream.
description-general: Velocity area station; approx. 60m wide in a straight section. The cableway was destroyed during a storm in 1998.
description-station-hydrometry: Natural bedrock control. Well calibrated. All flows contained. Weed growth apparent in May to September affecting low flows. Peak flow rating derived from current meter gaugings up to 3.6m (about 1.66 QMED), simple extrapolation beyond. One peak flow rating across period of record.
description-flow-record: Some monthly naturalised flows available. Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in August 2024 (WINFAP Files v13).
description-catchment: Predominantly upland catchment. Catchment drains from the Southern Uplands. Complex bedrock geology with Metamorphics and igneous rocks extensively overlain, in the lower half of the catchment, by superficial deposits, mainly Boulder Clay. Hill grazing is principal land use with some forestry and arable lands. Sparsely populated except for Lanark 5km u/s. Minimal floodplains. No significant catchment changes known.
description-flow-regime: Very minor net impact of artificial influences (some naturalised data) but flow pattern is affected by operation of upstream hydro-electric power station (Stonebyres Falls). Some small reservoirs in headwaters. Mining can affect low to medium flows.

name: Clyde at Sills of Clyde
description-summary: Velocity area station on the Clyde draining the Southern Uplands.
description-general: Velocity area station; about 15m wide section. Sited on a 200m straight natural reach between two sharp opposing bends. Flows are straight at cableway but there is some turbulence. Station transferred from SDD to Clyde RPB in Jul 1969.
description-station-hydrometry: Natural control. Low flow control is a riffle 30m d/s. At higher flows the remnants of two old mill weirs around 800m and 1.2km downstream may be influential. There is a five arch stone bridge 2.2km downstream that is likely the primary control during very big events. Weed growth in summer affects low flows. To date all flows contained. Peak flow ratings derived from current meter gaugings up to 2.9m (measured flow of 346 cumecs, which is around 1.7 QMED), with simple extrapolation beyond the highest gauging.
description-flow-record: Peak flows from October 1955. GDF from 1957. Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in September 2020 (WINFAP Files v9) and in August 2024 (WINFAP Files v13).
description-catchment: Upland catchment draining part of Southern Uplands, with several small storage reservoirs in headwaters. Silurian and Ordovician sedimentary rocks, approx. half of which overlain by superficial deposits, mainly Boulder Clay and sands and gravels. Land use: rough grazing, improved pasture, moorland, and afforestation. No significant catchment changes known.
description-flow-regime: Small storage reservoirs and one larger reservoir that feeds South Lanarkshire.

name: Clyde at Blairston
description-summary: Velocity area station on River Clyde in the Southern Uplands.
description-general: Velocity area station, about 60m wide. Velocity profile slightly uneven due to u/s bend. Steep grass and tree covered banks. Station is subject to vandalism, station burnt down Feb 1997, temporary logger installed (became permanent).
description-station-hydrometry: Control formed by piers of redundant rail bridge 300 m d/s. Less confidence in med-high flows than at Daldowie leading to occasional higher peaks at Blairston. Recorder moved from opposite bank in 1974. Peak flow rating derived from current meter gaugings up to 3.4m (1.8 QMED), just below max. recorded stage, simple extrapolation beyond.
description-flow-record: Rating change 01/07/1976 evident in flow pattern. Some monthly naturalised flows available (1958-1975). Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in September 2023 (WINFAP Files v12).
description-catchment: Predominantly upland catchment. Bedrock mainly Ordovician s'sts and shales. Lowther Hills in S are Silurian L'st, other upland areas Carboniferous basaltic lavas. The lower reaches of the catchment are overlain by superficial deposits, mainly Boulder Clay. Land use is mainly hill grazing and moorland on high ground, some afforestation; fruit farming in valley. Rapid urbanisation in lower catchment.
description-flow-regime: Several upland tributaries impounded for PWS. River hydropower schemes u/s of New Lanark; however this scheme does not involve damming, abstraction or diversion so exerts little or no influence on flow regime.

name: Kelvin at Bridgend
description-summary: Velocity area station. Station was closed in 1983 then re-opened in 1998 as a level only station.
description-general: Velocity area station, about 12m wide. River section 340m u/s of Inchbelly Bridge, Kirkintilloch. Station was closed in 1983 then re-opened in 1998 as a level only station. Removed from peak flows dataset in September 2019 (WINFAP Files v8).
description-station-hydrometry: Natural control. Station is affected by seasonal weed growth. Floods are contained within the banks which are heightened to protect fairly extensive low lying areas upstream. Peak flow rating derived from current meter gaugings up to 2.32m (0.5 QMED), simple extrapolation beyond. After dredging of river in 1976 rating was good fit, after 01/10/1979 however spot gaugings scatter substantially - no rating used from then.
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: Predominantly coal measures with some Dolerite and Basalt intrusions. Lowland river with some upland tributaries rising from Campsie Fells. Rough and improved pasture, some urban, small amount of forestry. No significant catchment changes known.
description-flow-regime: Responsive regime. Some small reservoirs and lochs in headwaters. Forth and Clyde Canal fed from some reservoirs.

name: South Calder Water at Forgewood
description-summary: Compound crump profile weir on the South Calder Water, closed in May 2010.
description-general: Compound Crump profile weir (centre: 3.7m, flanks: 13.4m). Gradient sufficient to avoid drowning. Vandalism poses a problem. Station closed May 2010.
description-station-hydrometry: All flows contained. Theoretical rating confirmed by low flow gaugings up to 0.495m (about 0.06 QMED). Depositions u/s of right flank of weir causing accretion of bank, intermittently dug out in the past.
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: Relatively subdued topography developed on sedimentary formations of Carboniferous age (chiefly Coal Measures); predominantly overlain by superficial deposits. Land use arable and pasture with some woodland and urbanised areas - the gauging station is located in Motherwell. Large steelworks closed down in mid-90s, hence less water abstraction at Ravenscraig.
description-flow-regime: Flow pattern influenced by industrial abstractions and discharges - net import of water from the Clyde.

name: Rotten Calder Water at Redlees
description-summary: Compound Crump profile weir on Rotten Calder Water.
description-general: Compound Crump profile weir (central crest: 1.8m, flanks: 4.9m). Occasional vandalism. Removed from peak flows dataset in August 2021 (WINFAP Files v10).
description-station-hydrometry: River gradient obviates drowning. Tree debris is a problem and can cause blockage of centre of crump weir. All flows contained. Theoretical rating confirmed by low flow gaugings up to 0.2m (about 0.013 QMED). Data removed from peak flows dataset because station not designed or operated for flood estimation as well as problems with wood and urban debris in weir.
description-flow-record: Data for 07/08/08-24/09/08 dubious due to weir blockage.
description-catchment: A mainly impervious catchment (Carboniferous deposits predominate; Drift cover). Moorland and hill pasture in the headwaters, some significant urban growth in the lower catchment (East Kilbride).
description-flow-regime: Runoff augmented by sewage and industrial effluent.

name: Nethan at Kirkmuirhill
description-summary: Compound crump profile weir. Flows affected by PWS abstractions.
description-general: Compound Crump profile weir (centre crest: 2.4m, flanks: 4.3m); significant accretion u/s of rh crest. Removed from peak flows dataset in February 2018 (WINFAP Files v6).
description-station-hydrometry: Flows remain modular and are fully contained; the channel is deeply incised into rock. Wood debris causes periodic problems. Theoretical rating confirmed by low flow gaugings up to 0.215m (about 0.011 QMED).
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: The Nethan drains from Nutberry Hill. Complex geology - mostly ORS and Carboniferous limestone overlain by peat in the headwaters and Boulder Clay in the lower reaches. Mainly impervious catchment. The land use is a mixture of improved and rough pasture with some small reservoirs and forest cover. Afforestation in the headwaters, hill pasture below. Open cast mining.
description-flow-regime: Runoff is diminished by PWS abstractions.

name: Gryfe at Craigend
description-summary: Velocity area station. Flows significantly affected by Loch Thom and Gryfe Reservoir in the west.
description-general: Velocity area station about 20m wide with curving broad-crested masonry weir control on gentle bend.
description-station-hydrometry: The weir crest is 0.24m high and drowns out at mid to high flows. With respect to flow calibration, the left bank forms the outer bend and hence is more influential than the right bank. The left bank is poorly defined with the profile opening up into a wider section above around 1m, where nearly all the flow is contained within the span of the cableway. The highest flood gauging at 2.145m on 30/12/15, measured a flow of 134.8 cumecs and is thought to have captured nearly all the flow. This flood gauging is over double the flow of the next highest gauging and hence was used to inform the revision of all the ratings through the station history during a period of record rating review exercise carried out in 2024. The insensitivity of the broad crested weir is not conducive to accurate low flow estimation. The limitations of this station producing accurate low flow estimations are further compounded by periods of control instability, with intermittent erosion and bypassing around the left-wing wall and a period of weir collapse. The left bank at the weir has been subject to intermittent periods of erosion, where in between various repair attempts, a small percentage of flow has passed around the weir. These periods where the control is altered are largely compensated by low end rating adjustments. The weir crest began to break up around November 1996 and this prompted mitigating works to create a temporary state of repair between 01/04/1997 and 15/02/2000. This period is marked by an elevated stage, increased gauging scatter and reduced confidence in flow estimation through the entire flow range. The upper end of the calibration in this period is based on the curve of the flood segment over the weir in its normal state with an alpha adjustment to align the rating with the parallel shift observed in the low to mid-range gaugings. Some doubt on the correct trajectory of the rating top end means there is low confidence in the estimation of floods in this period and Peak Flow estimates from WY1996 to WY1999 are flagged as rejected for this reason. Low flows in this period are also of much lower confidence, compounded by a confusing record of stage edits and adjustments to the stage at which gaugings were referenced. There is a record of the gauge datum being lowered from 11.25m to 11.243m around 01/02/1997. The shift was likely applied to allow positive stage recording as the weir crest progressively broke up. This datum shift is not obvious in the stage record and has likely been smoothed out during the stage editing process. Additionally, a significant rating change is applied two months later to reflect the works to repair the weir starting on 01/04/1997. For these reasons, a rating adjustment is not deemed necessary to cover the two-month period between the datum shift and the start of the weir repair.
description-flow-record: Some monthly naturalised flows (1964-74). Peak flows rejected between Water Year 1996/1997 and Water Year 1999/2000, during weir repair. Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in August 2025 (WINFAP Files v14).
description-catchment: Wet, responsive upland catchment draining from Duchal Moor. Geology: Carboniferous basaltic lavas; isolated pockets of Boulder Clay in valleys. Extensive cover of raised beach deposits W of gauging site. Land use: predominantly grazing, some forestry. Urban development along valley. No significant catchment changes known.
description-flow-regime: Responsive. Significant affect of L. Thom and Gryfe Res. in W. Runoff augmented by compensation flows and spillages from reservoired catchment (11.6 sq.km).

name: White Cart Water at Hawkhead
description-summary: Velocity area station with complex water utilisation.
description-general: Velocity area station; approx. 20m wide section in a straight reach of uniform cross-section. Occasional vandalism.
description-station-hydrometry: Major flood defence works have been developed through the White Cart catchment. In the first phase, three flood storage areas were built in the upper catchment. This work started in March 2008 and were completed in Autumn 2010. A second phase of the flood defence involved the construction of flood defence walls along the White Cart in the Southside of Glasgow upstream of Hawkhead Gauging Station. This work started in January 2009 and was completed in October 2011.
description-flow-record: Complex water utilisation; some monthly naturalised flows available (1963-74). Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in April 2017 (WINFAP Files v5).
description-catchment: Predominantly lowland catchment. Carboniferous rocks (basalt in the headwaters) dominate; greater than half overlain by Boulder Clay. Much of the catchment is open pasture (with several small lochs) but the northern part is heavily urbanised (Glasgow); some forestry. Notable floodplains. Development of East Kilbride and Newton Mearns (suburban development). Flood prevention scheme planned for the future.
description-flow-regime: Storage in the catchment with complex water utilisation. Urban drainage systems.

name: Clyde at Daldowie
description-summary: Velocity area station. Small influence of hydroelectric scheme at New Lanark.
description-general: Velocity area station with cableway; approx. 50m wide section. Lowest on the Clyde.
description-station-hydrometry: Natural channel control. Well calibrated. Bypassing of flow can occur on right bank behind station hut at floods above 3.5m. These flows are occasionally gauged from the ramp/walkway. Occasional vandalism and problems with woody debris. There is a very large weir at Carmyle approximately 2.1km downstream from Daldowie that will likely act as a control at high flows at least. The weir has a rectangular notch where a sluice gate would have been, but is now permantly open. The piers of an old railway bridge and a tight bend in the river may also be influential in the control during flood events. Multiple peak flow ratings applied across period of record.
description-flow-record: Some monthly naturalised flows available (1967-74). Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in September 2019 (WINFAP Files v8) and in August 2024 (WINFAP Files v13).
description-catchment: Large catchment with upland headwaters. Mixed bedrock geology - Ordovician (in the south) to Carboniferous with superficial deposits, mainly Boulder Clay, below the headwaters. Hill pasture is the major land use in the moorland headwaters with some forestry. Mixed farming and urbanisation in the lower valley. In last 5 years, sewage of smaller towns, e.g. East Kilbride, transferred to Daldowie STW.
description-flow-regime: Some reservoirs in headwaters (Daer Reservoir). Small influence of hydroelectric scheme at New Lanark.

name: Avon Water at Fairholm
description-summary: Velocity area station on the Avon Water.
description-general: Velocity area station; approx. 25m wide section in a very straight uniform reach.
description-station-hydrometry: Rock platform below a bridge forms the control. All but the highest flows are contained. Two ratings due to a datum shift of 3ft (0.914m) on 01/03/72. The pre 01/03/72 rating is based on gaugings up to 100 cumecs and a modelled out of bank segment has been added. The post 01/03/72 rating is based on gaugings up to 200 cumecs, with a modelled out of bank segment added.
description-flow-record: Some monthly naturalised flows (1964-74). Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in October 2018 (WINFAP Files v7).
description-catchment: Predominantly upland catchment. Mostly ORS and Carboniferous formations extensively overlain by superficial deposits; mainly Boulder Clay with peat in the headwaters. Land use hill grazing, moorland, rough and improved pasture, and some forest cover. No significant catchment changes known.
description-flow-regime: Flashy response. Two small reservoirs in the catchment but flow pattern remains responsive.

name: Kelvin at Dryfield
description-summary: Velocity area station in the low lying central valley of Scotland. Bypassing occurs in largest events.
description-general: Velocity area station; approx. 30m wide river section. Recorder sited in straight even reach where erosion has made banks very steep. The river was canalised during last war and floodbanks made on both banks from dredged material. Cableway installed in 1960 so no high measurements prior to this date. From July 1998 maintained as level only station for flood warning purposes.
description-station-hydrometry: The section is affected by weed growth and requires constant attention. Peak flow ratings derived from current meter gaugings up to 3.5m (about 1.1 QMED), simple extrapolation beyond. Bypassing at the very highest flows is a significant problem with the rating.
description-flow-record: Bypassing occurs in largest events (e.g. Sep 1985, Dec 1994), overtopping at both banks. Flows rejected from July 1998 because of the maintainance of the station as level only for flood warning purposes. Via correlation with the downstream gauge 84001 the highest recorded event is greatly underestimated at Dryfield.
description-catchment: Catchment in the low lying central valley of Scotland. Upland catchments drain from the Campsie Fells. Millstone Grit and coal bearing rocks of Carboniferous age overlain by extensive Boulder Clay and sand and gravels deposits. Mixed land use including farming, forestry, urban development and open cast mining. Flood prevention schemes along the river at Kirkintilloch.
description-flow-regime: The river was canalised during the last war downstream of Kilsyth. The Forth and Clyde canal is influenced by feeder reservoirs at low flow.

name: Luggie Water at Condorrat
description-summary: Velocity area station in a catchment with significant urban development.
description-general: Velocity area approx. 8m wide section with compound broad-crested weir, central low flow notch, about 8m wide. Cableway and weir installed in March 1968. Occasional vandalism.
description-station-hydrometry: Bypassing occurs at the very highest flows (e.g. Dec 1994). Once the weir drowns out, the higher flows will be influenced by a wooden footbridge downstream that has a flat bottom at bank level. This footbridge has been built sometime in the period of record. Before the construction of the footbridge the higher floods will have been controlled by the humpback stone road bridge further downstream. Peak flow ratings derived from current meter gaugings up to 1.5m (about 0.9 QMED), simple extrapolation beyond. Gauging evidence shows a large rating shift that has been assigned an arbitrary date of 01/01/98. A review of the ratings and available station records highlighted some historic operational issues at the site such as slumping of the ramp gauge and poor quality gaugings.
description-flow-record: Although the site has been operational since 17/11/62, SEPA does not hold data prior to March 1968 and a note in the records suggest the pre 1968 data was of poor quality. Peak flow data rejected pre-1998 due to issues with rating derivation described under 'Hydrometry'.
description-catchment: Lowland catchment. Predominantly Coal Measures with intrusive basalt overlain extensively by Boulder Clay, some peat in the headwaters. Much of the catchment is agricultural in character with significant urban development in the north (Cumbernauld), and some forestry. No controlled storages but significant local depressions and boggy areas. Housing development encroaching on right bank floodplain d/s.
description-flow-regime: No abstractions in catchment. Minor influences at low flows from open cast mining. The deep coal mines were closed prior to station opening.

name: Black Cart Water at Milliken Park
description-summary: Velocity area station. Flows significantly affected by operation of Castle Semple Loch and Barr Loch (fed by Calder Water).
description-general: Velocity area station about 27m wide.
description-station-hydrometry: Station has informal (dished) concrete low flow control of length 26.52m and natural high flow control. Overtopping of rb can occur when stage exceeds 1m. Peak flow ratings derived from current meter gaugings up to 1.1 m (about QMED), simple extrapolation beyond (stable rating). Problems with winch resulted in bad gaugings in early 1990s. Multiple peak flow ratings across period of record.
description-flow-record: Flow control evident on the hydrograph trace, although less obvious post 1980. Monthly naturalised flows available (1967-74). Site was recalibrated back to 2001 during the 2010 review, mainly affecting low flows. Station started operating on 10/01/1967, data reliable from 01/12/1967. Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in August 2024 (WINFAP Files v13).
description-catchment: Predominantly lowland, wet, catchment. Principally impervious - Carboniferous basalt and igneous intrusions, overlain by Boulder Clay. Peat in some upland areas, river gravel on floodplains. Rural land use, urbanisation in valley; some forestry. No significant catchment changes known.
description-flow-regime: Several lochs and reservoirs (e.g. Rowbanks) provide storage, flows sig. affected by operation of Castle Semple Loch and Barr Loch (fed by Calder Water). 75% of the catchment is controlled by Castle Semple Loch.

name: Clyde at Tulliford Mill
description-summary: Velocity area station on the River Clyde.
description-general: Velocity area station; approx. 60m wide.
description-station-hydrometry: Natural open channel control. Weed growth at low flows affects the Clyde from May to September. Banks are likely overtopped during extreme events. A major rating shift is applied on 18/10/2011, Pre 18/10/2011, one flood segment is applied to various lower segments and is gauged up to 2.543m (measured flow of 372.4 cumecs) with simple extrapolation beyond. Post 18/10/2011, a new flood segment is applied to ratings, based on gaugings up to 2.230m (measured flow of 313.9 cumecs) with simple extrapolation beyond. The reason for the change in flood control is currently unknown and the rating change is based purely on gauging evidence.
description-flow-record: Monthly naturalised flows available (1969-1974). Flows from Jan 1978 reprocessed in 2013. Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in September 2023 (WINFAP Files v12).
description-catchment: The catchment ranges in height from 180-800m. Mixed geology - ancient sedimentaries (ORS/Ordovician) dominate the headwaters; mostly igneous formations below. Substantial superficial deposits. About one third is cultivated, the remainder is hill grazing and moorland, with some forestry. No significant catchment changes known. Small reservoirs in headwaters.
description-flow-regime: Catchment includes a number of PWS gathering grounds from which the yield is exported.

name: North Calder Water at Calderpark
description-summary: Velocity area station in central lowlands east of Glasgow.
description-general: Velocity area station; about 12m wide section. The recorder is sited in a river bend, which creates a asymmetrical velocity profile. Outer bank is a steep cliff being undercut by river. The inner bank is quite steep.
description-station-hydrometry: The station was built with a broad crested weir in 1962, and then the weir was removed on 09/10/1972. The datum was lowered by 2 feet on 01/04/1972; likely in preparation for the weir removal. There is no rating archived that represents the datum and control change between April and October 1972 and more investigation is required to validate the details in this period. The cableway was removed due to landslip and fallen tree on 24/07/1990. All flows are contained. The post 1972 rating is derived from current meter gaugings up to 1.360m (measured flow of 25.5cumecs) with simple extrapolation beyond.
description-flow-record: No POTs between 1968 and 1973 and during this period peak flows are lower than gauged daily flows. Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in September 2023 (WINFAP Files v12).
description-catchment: Lies in central lowlands east of Glasgow. Contains several small storage lochs. Sedimentary rocks of Carboniferous age; approx. 95% of which is overlain by superficial deposits. Land use: grassland, forestry, arable lands u/s; extensive urban area d/s. No significant catchment changes known. However changes in sewage discharges and abstraction policy of Scottish Water might have occurred and would have an impact on low flows.
description-flow-regime: Many artificial influences which mainly impact on low to medium flows. Contains several storage reservoirs for canal supply. Monkland Canal drains through catchment and affects low flows. Water is also exported to Forth & Clyde Canal.

name: Glazert Water at Milton of Campsie
description-summary: Velocity area station in a flashy catchment.
description-general: Velocity area station.
description-station-hydrometry: The control is a compound weir of the Clyde River Purification Board design with two outer broad-crested sections straddling a rectangular flume style low flow channel. Archive notes describe the breakpoint of the low flow notch is at 0.36m and the structure drowns out at 1.5m. The weir suffered from erosion, and records describe the 1990 spates as being of particular affect. By 2023 the base of the low flow section was worn down to the concrete rebars, prompting some repair work between 19/07/2023 ad 24/10/2023. These repair works replaced the low flow channel and added a concrete layer (100mm) on top of the existing downstream aprons, increasing their height by 0.100m. The crest height of the two side sections weas unaltered during these works. The gauge zero was inadvertently changed after the installation of a new ramp gauge in 2002. The exact date and size of shift is pending further investigation of SEPA records but gauging deviations indicate it was lowered in the order of 0.060m and the corresponding rating start date suggests it happened on 11/09/2002. The ramp was replaced again in conjunction with weir repair works between July and October 2023, with no datum shift. Peak flow rating derived from current meter gaugings up to 1.830, with a measured flow of 50.6 cumecs. All flows are contained in the channel.
description-flow-record: Some monthly naturalised flows available (1970-74). Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in August 2025 (WINFAP Files v14).
description-catchment: Catchment topography is >1/3 lowland, <2/3 upland, draining the Campsie Fells. Carboniferous series (principally the Scottish Carboniferous L'st) dominate the bedrock - overlain by mixed superficial deposits. Sparsely populated. Landuse mainly rough pasture and improved pasture in lower parts; some forestry. No significant lochs or storages. No significant catchment changes known.
description-flow-regime: Flashy response. Minimal effluent returns affecting low flows.

name: Duneaton at Maidencots
description-summary: A velocity-area station in an upland catchment.
description-general: Velocity area station.
description-station-hydrometry: Ragged rock bar control - considered to be stable and sensitive. Bypassing is unlikely.
description-flow-record: Some early flow data available from 1966.
description-catchment: An upland catchment developed mainly on ORS (and older) formations; approx. 50% overlain by Boulder Clay. Mostly grasslands with some forestry.
description-flow-regime: No significant storages or (current) abstractions.

name: Bothlin Burn at Auchengeich
description-summary: Crump single-crested weir with flow pattern affected by motorway runoff and STW effluent.
description-general: Crump (triangular profile) single-crested weir. No gaugings available to verify rating above structure full. Removed from peak flows dataset in September 2023 (WINFAP Files v12).
description-station-hydrometry: Flow contained over the full range. There is some siltation behind the weir. Theoretical rating confirmed by low flow gaugings to 0.18m (about 0.11 QMED).
description-flow-record: Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in August 2021 (WINFAP Files v10).
description-catchment: A small undulating catchment, containing three old mining villages, developed on Scottish Carboniferous L'st overlain with superficial deposits (approx. 80% Boulder Clay). Significantly urbanised with grassland, pasture, wetlands and some forestry. Small lochs in the catchment headwaters. Building of the M73 and M80 motorway (1970s).
description-flow-regime: Sensibly natural regime but motorway (M73) runoff and STW effluent may influence flow pattern.

name: North Calder Water at Hillend
description-summary: A station with artificial flows controlled by reservoir releases.
description-general: Flat V fibre-glass Crump weir. Station closed May 2010.
description-station-hydrometry: Weir susceptible to minor weed growth in summer. Channel flooded out at extreme high flows (very rare).
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: Bedrock geology mainly Upper and Lower Coal Measures, with some quartz-dolerite intrusions. Significant cover; mainly Boulder Clay and peat. Mixed land use with significant proportion of lochs (>9%).
description-flow-regime: Flow is totally artificial, being controlled by releases from Hillend Res. (but flood releases via second spillway bypass).

name: Luggie Water at Oxgang
description-summary: Velocity area station in a catchment of mixed land use, some urbanisation.
description-general: Velocity area station; about 10m wide. Station removed from peak flows dataset in August 2024 (WINFAP Files v13).
description-station-hydrometry: Informal Flat V triangular profile weir control. Some sign of weir undercutting in 1992, not thought to affect flows. Two peak flow ratings derived from current meter gaugings, pre- and post-Jan 1980. Both have spot gaugings up to about 0.5 QMED, simple extrapolation beyond.
description-flow-record: Most flows contained but some spillage in flood conditions (e.g. Dec 1994).
description-catchment: Catchment is generally lowland and undulating. Predominantly Coal Measures with some dolerite and basalt intrusions extensively overlain by superficial deposits, mainly Boulder Clay. Mixed land use, farming, urban development and open cast mining. Urban development (Cumbernauld) d/s of the station in late 1970s leading to a shift in channel morphology.
description-flow-regime: Until 2003, sewage discharge to Bothlin Burn joining u/s of station.

name: Allander Water at Milngavie
description-summary: Velocity area station. The catchment contains a number of natural and artificial storages but the flow regime remains responsive.
description-general: Velocity area station; 8m wide section. Operated by SDD as a level-only station from 1960's until SEPA took over on 01/11/1972.
description-station-hydrometry: Station has flat V triangular profile weir for low flow control (installed 01/02/1973). Gravel build-up on weir has been observed throughout the stations history. Gravel is subject to reworking and therefore the weir is not providing a stable control through time. There is low confidence in flood estimations above around 10 cumecs prior to August 2007 due to the limited range of gauging evidence collected. A 2.526m spate on 18/08/2007 resulted in a shift in the stations flood flow control and a new calibration was created. The post 2007 calibration results in flows with greater confidence, however, a still limited gauging range (21 cumecs gauged vs 55 cumecs highest on record flow) limits this stations usability to QMED only. Two peak flow ratings across period of record.
description-flow-record: QHigh_1973.2 was developed for 1973 to 2007, but limited gaugings result in low confidence in the flood calibration. The published data therefore excludes Peak Flow data prior to WY 2007. Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in August 2026 (WINFAP Files v15).
description-catchment: Hilly catchment developed mostly on Carboniferous formations (basaltic lava and Scottish Carboniferous L'st predominate); overlain by Boulder Clay in the lower catchment. Upland grazing is the main land use; some afforestation and also urban development (Milngavie) near the outfall. No significant catchment changes known.
description-flow-regime: The catchment contains a number of natural and artificial storages but the flow regime remains responsive.

name: North Calder Water at Calderbank
description-summary: A station in an urbanised catchment with canal offtake just u/s.
description-general: Canal offtake just u/s. Station closed February 2005.
description-station-hydrometry: Fibre-glass flume for low flows, broad-crested control for higher flows. Flume is susceptible to blockage by vandals (but checked daily). High flow calibration is poorly defined - further gauging planned.
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: Urbanised catchment with rough grazing remaining on uplands. Reservoired headwaters. Bedrock principally Upper and Lower Coal Measures overlain by Boulder Clay and localised riverine deposits.
description-flow-regime: NA

name: Cander Water at Candermill
description-summary: A station on a tributary in the River Clyde catchment.
description-general: NA
description-station-hydrometry: Non-standard Flat V and broad-crested control, no wing walls; current meter calibration. Flood flows spill onto banks. High flow rating under review following road works involving the rb. New rating from 30/07/2002 following July 2002 storm event that redefined channel.
description-flow-record: July 2002 storm event redefined channel.
description-catchment: Small, northward draining, rural catchment developed on productive Coal Measures, with ORS (Greywacke Conglomerate) occurring on some hills. Boulder Clay and terrace gravels along the Cander Water. Quarrying activity in S. of catchment.
description-flow-regime: Responsive flow regime.

name: White Cart Water at Overlee
description-summary: A station to the south of Glasgow with rapid urbanisation in the lower catchment.
description-general: Thin-plate damaged and removed in 1999.
description-station-hydrometry: Rectangular thin-plate low flow notch in a broad-crested (V cross-section) weir. Confirmatory gaugings not yet available for the full flow range. Good fall below weir, flows remain modular.
description-flow-record: Poor low flow gauging section, reflected in occasional higher flows recorded than at 84012 (e.g. Jun 2010 HIF).
description-catchment: Geology - mostly basaltic lava and Carboniferous L'st overlain with Boulder Clay and river gravels along main river channel. Land use - predominantly grazing but rapid urbanisation of lower catchment and upper catchment is becoming forested.
description-flow-regime: Frequent flooding d/s of the gauge reflects flashy nature of the river. There are several reservoirs and lochs within the catchment.

name: Watstone Burn at Watstone
description-summary: Station opened to study the Burn because of proposed new town at Stonehouse.
description-general: Crump weir. Station opened to study the Burn because of proposed new town at Stonehouse. Station closed in 1981, re-opened 1986-93.
description-station-hydrometry: NA
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: Geology: predominantly Carboniferous deposits overlain with Boulder Clay; ORS (Greywacke conglomerate) occurs on some hills. Rural catchment.
description-flow-regime: No significant abstractions or discharges, however, proportion of runoff diverted out of catchment (due to urban drainage).

name: Bagabout Burn at Giffnock
description-summary: A station located within Giffnock STW.
description-general: Located in Giffnock STW. Station closed.
description-station-hydrometry: Rectangular thin-plate weir, overtops at 0.17m.
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: Small, urban catchment. Bedrock: extrusive igneous rocks overlain with Boulder Clay, and some isolated Upper Limestone outcrops.
description-flow-regime: No significant abstractions or discharges.

name: White Cart Water at MacQuisten Bridge
description-summary: Flood warning station on the White Cart Water, closed in August 2010.
description-general: Velocity area station with well confined open channel. Station closed August 2010.
description-station-hydrometry: Catchment prone to frequent flooding.
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: Outcrops of Carboniferous Coal Measures and basalts overlain by significant superficial deposits, mainly Boulder Clay. Rural catchment undergoing land use changes: afforestation in upper reaches and rapid urban expansion of East Kilbride and Castlemilk.
description-flow-regime: Very responsive, natural regime. A number of small PWS reservoirs in upper reaches but have insignificant effect at station.

name: Kittoch Water at Waterside
description-summary: A velocity-area flood warning station, on the edge of Glasgow. A significant percentage of the catchment drains the large new town of East Kilbridge .
description-general: Velocity area station. Flood warning station. Station added to peak flows dataset in September 2019 (WINFAP Files v8).
description-station-hydrometry: Multiple peak flow ratings across period of record, based on gaugings.
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: Carboniferous Coal Measures and outcrops of Basalt extensively overlain by Boulder Clay. Small, rural catchment having undergone rapid land use change since the expansion of East Kilbride in the 1960s.
description-flow-regime: Very minor impact from sewage works u/s of catchment. The urban drainage system produces misleading water balance.

name: Douglas Water at Happendon
description-summary: A station in a rural catchment whose high flows should be treated with caution.
description-general: Crump weir. All flows contained.
description-station-hydrometry: Rating altered as a result of damage to structure during Jan 2010 event. Rating extrapolated above 25 cumecs and higher flows should be treated with caution.
description-flow-record: Freezing of stilling well evident Jan, Dec 2010; record HIF in Jan 2010 reflects ice melt.
description-catchment: Carboniferous rocks with local occurrences of Lower ORS, intruded by basaltic and doleritic dykes. Significant superficial deposit cover (mainly Boulder Clay). Rural catchment having undergone some afforestation.
description-flow-regime: Two small lochs in catchment but flow pattern remains responsive.

name: Clyde at Abington
description-summary: Station built to improve flood warning in the Clyde catchment.
description-general: Velocity area station, the most upstream on the Clyde. Station added to peak flows dataset in August 2021 (WINFAP Files v10).
description-station-hydrometry: Station spills into right floodplain after around 2m and then into left floodplain after around 2.8m. Rating based on gaugings up to ~1.6m and thereafter higher flow estimates are informed by velocity indexing from a fixed ADCP and floodplain modelling.
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: Heavily grazed uplands and heather moor. Large wind farms have been installed in the catchment since the station was built.
description-flow-regime: Two major reservoirs in the catchment.

name: Leven at Linnbrane
description-summary: Velocity area station substantially regulated during summer.
description-general: Velocity area station, about 35m wide.
description-station-hydrometry: Stable open channel control with low flow recalibration only required after suspected erosion from the 1990 floods, and then another low-end adjustment following the 2006 flood. The peak flow rating is calibrated using gaugings up to 2.536m, with a measured flow of 156 cumecs. Flows are largely contained in the channel. The datum was raised by 1m in June 1982 during the installation of the first metric ramp, raising the gauge zero from 4.298 mAOD to 5.298 mAOD. The stage record has been edited to show the datum shift at midnight on 01/07/1982. The ramp was replaced on 07/06/1984. A survey in 2003 measured the gauge zero of the 1984 ramp as being 5.264 mAOD. This slight difference in value from the previous figure by -0.034m may reflect the error band around the surveys of 1982 and 2003, or it may indicate that the 1984 gauge was installed to a different level. There no gaugings between 1982 and 1984 to evaluate this and the contemporary ratings do not show a shift in the expected direction. As there is no obvious shift in the stage record on 07/06/1984, the notion of datum shift on 07/06/1984 can effectively be ignored.
description-flow-record: A problem with the gauging winch was identified, which means that all gaugings between 1991-2000 should be viewed as suspect. Naturalised monthly flows available (1963-74). Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in August 2025 (WINFAP Files v14).
description-catchment: Large, wet, upland catchment with mountainous headwaters, often snowy in winter. Bedrock geology dominated by ancient metamorphic formations - overlain by superficial deposits in the west. The land use is rough pasture and moorland u/s, improved pasture d/s, small amount of arable land, some forestry. Several water bodies. The catchment outflow is controlled by Loch Lomond (surface area 71sq.km).
description-flow-regime: Natural regime until loch outfall control weir built in 1971, now substantially regulated during summer. Barrage does not operate in winter, and does not affect high flows. Three main lochs are located in catchment - Loch Sloy with a hydroelectric power scheme, Loch Lomond with barrage (which may affect flow) and Loch Arklet. All three provide a PWS.

name: Endrick Water at Gaidrew
description-summary: Velocity area station in an upland rural catchment, draining from the Campsie Fells. Flows affected by export of water from Carron Res. into the Forth system.
description-general: Velocity area station, approx. 28m wide.
description-station-hydrometry: Natural channel control. Low and medium flows considered reliable but flood discharges are of a lesser accuracy (due to overspill on to the lb floodplain above 3.6m and a curved approach to the measuring reach). Peak flow ratings before and after datum change in May 1981 derived from current meter gaugings. Pre-1981 gaugings up to about 0.7 QMED, post-1981 up to about QMED, simple extrapolation beyond. The rating changed in October 2008 following significant channel scour event where gaugings up to 50cumecs showed considerable deviation from earlier ratings. Multiple peak flow ratings across period of record.
description-flow-record: Flows over 60 cumecs should presently be regarded with caution. Some monthly naturalised flows available (1967-74). Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in August 2024 (WINFAP Files v13).
description-catchment: An upland rural catchment, draining from the Campsie Fells, developed on ORS overlain with Boulder Clay; large tracts of sand and gravel also. Land use: mostly moorland, rough grazing, pasture; forestry and some limited cropland. No significant catchment changes known.
description-flow-regime: Runoff is diminished by the export of water from Carron Res. into the Forth system.

name: Falloch at Glen Falloch
description-summary: Velocity area station in a very responsive, natural catchment.
description-general: Velocity area station, approx. 35m wide.
description-station-hydrometry: Long broad-crested weir (with rectangular notch) as low flow control - installed Feb 1975. Damage to part of main crest results in a small discharge bypassing the central notch. Very high flows above 2.4m could bypass station on either side. Peak flow ratings derived from current meter gaugings, simple extrapolation beyond. Ratings reviewed in 2016.
description-flow-record: Full period of record peak flow data reviewed and released in April 2017 (WINFAP Files v5).
description-catchment: Very wet, mountainous, catchment draining southern slopes of Benn Oss and northern slopes of Beinn a Chroin and Beinn Chabair, often snowy in winter. Developed on ancient metamorphic formations with isolated outcrops of igneous intrusions (impermeable). Peat deposits in upland areas. Small lochans in some headwaters, but have little affect on flows. Land use mainly moorland and rough grazing with small amounts of forestry. Minimal floodplains. No significant catchment changes known.
description-flow-regime: Very responsive regime. No significant abstractions or discharges.

name: Luss Water at Luss
description-summary: A velocity-area station near the shore of Loch Lomond with a very responsive, natural regime.
description-general: Velocity area station.
description-station-hydrometry: Artificial low flow control: broad-crested weir with low flow notch, slight damage to centre section repaired in autumn 1992. Rating validated by gaugings from 0.15 - 5 cumecs, with historical gaugings to c.25 cumecs. However weir is now in poor condition.
description-flow-record: Numerous record gaps May 1983 - 1987 due to site access issues. No daily flow data for January - June 2013 due to weir repairs.
description-catchment: A very wet, mountainous catchment developed mainly on Dalradian schists, overlain by Boulder Clay. Land use is mostly grassland.
description-flow-regime: Very responsive, natural regime.

name: Little Eachaig at Dalinlongart
description-summary: Velocity area station in a compact, steep, mountainous catchment with a very responsive flow regime.
description-general: Velocity area station; approx. 17m wide. Cableway on site until 1988.
description-station-hydrometry: Compound artificial control (low flow notch, broad-crested flanks). At high flows weir is drowned and control is natural channel. All flows contained to date. Peak flow ratings derived using meter gaugings up to 0.8m (about 0.3 QMED), simple extrapolation beyond. Based on cableway spot gaugings up to 1988.
description-flow-record: NA
description-catchment: A compact, steep, mountainous catchment, often snowy in winter - very wet - developed on ancient metamorphic formations; overlain by limited superficial deposits. Landuse mainly forest and moorland. Minimal floodplains. No significant catchment changes known, however ongoing forestry operations in catchment.
description-flow-regime: Natural flow regime but catchwaters divert a small runoff volume to Loch Tarsan. Very responsive flow regime. There are also some minor industrial and agricultural abstractions.

name: Eachaig at Eckford
description-summary: Velocity area station. Loch Eck dominates catchment.
description-general: Velocity area station, about 28m wide. Station closed 31/05/98.
description-station-hydrometry: Riffle control for low to medium flows. Natural channel control at high flows. All but major floods were contained within the channel, but some bypassing on lb. The river channel at the station had been significantly changing during the 1980s. Apparently material had been dumped into the channel u/s to reinforce the river adjacent to a caravan site. This was thought to have caused erosion of the far bank at the station. Peak flow ratings derived using current meter gaugings up to 1.7m (0.8 QMED), simple extrapolation beyond. Ratings applied only until July 1991 due to unreliable data thereafter.
